text: A man who has spent a few years in New York has decided he is a Yankee, and when his wife arrives from Russia he sets about correcting her. The correction is the trouble. Around them the Lower East Side of the 1890s is almost entirely Jewish, so nothing he performs is demanded by the street; it is demanded by him, in a rented room, across ninety minutes that stay indoors with a marriage rather than widening into a panorama of immigration. Joan Micklin Silver keeps the comedy of manners close to the humiliation inside it: accent, dress, the words chosen for ordinary things. His wife arrives unable to read the arrangement she has walked into, and begins to read it fast. The National Film Registry took the film in later; in 1975 it was a small production about two people arguing over who they are permitted to be.

The mainland is offering a future, and some of the islanders decline it. Michael Powell gives that refusal seventy-five minutes and takes it seriously rather than filing it as stubbornness, which obliges the film to make the case for a place whose economy has already stopped working: rock, water, weather, and a shrinking number of people to divide the labor among. The romance runs inside an argument about evacuation, so courtship keeps colliding with the question of whether anyone will remain to live nearby. American critics put it among the National Board of Review's ten best of 1938, an odd fate for a British picture without stars, set in a community that is emptying. Nothing in it is raised to a lament. The men argue about boats and grazing and the future in the flat voices of people who have argued before.

Fifteen years in an asylum, and then his own front door. The veteran at the center of A Bill of Divorcement comes back to a household that has gone on doing ordinary arithmetic without him: a wife with new arrangements, a daughter grown and days from her wedding. George Cukor allows the situation seventy minutes and very little air. It plays as a series of conversations in rooms where everyone must decide quickly what is owed to a man who is family on paper and a stranger in practice. Scholars have since read Cukor for doubling, and the pairing here needs no excavating: the father's history and the daughter's future keep being described in the same words. What holds the thing together is her willingness to look straight at what she has been handed, while the adults negotiate around it.

The government paid for it, then decided the public should not see it; the film waited until 1981. John Huston's fifty-eight minutes sit inside a military hospital with men whose injuries left nothing visible, and with the staff trying to talk them back toward speech, sleep, steadiness. The vocabulary of 1946 was psychoneurosis and shell shock; the condition is the one now called PTSD. The method is mostly to hold on a face while a man attempts to finish a sentence, and that appears to have been the problem: a film made for internal Army use had produced footage in which the war's cost was legible on the men who had won it. Two dates now sit on it, 1946 and 1981, and the gap between them has become part of what the film is.

Ten thousand children left Europe in the nine months before the war began, put onto trains by parents who stayed behind. Mark Jonathan Harris gives the transports two hours, long enough for the number to stop being a number: a suitcase, a label, an address in England, a foster family assigned by strangers, a language to be acquired in a hurry. Rescue and injury were the same event here, and the film declines to resolve that. Most of what it holds is the memory of small logistics, what was packed, what was said on the platform, whose name was on the list and whose was not, recalled decades later by people who were children at the time. It took the Academy's award for documentary feature, though its actual subject is the price of having been saved.

Between sets, the camera goes off to look at the water. Newport, summer of 1958: a jazz festival, a town full of visitors, an audience watched as closely as the bandstand. Bert Stern lets the day set the structure, so the film moves from afternoon improvisation to gospel after dark, and the organizing principle is the changing light rather than a running order of names. Concert films usually argue for the importance of the music. This one is more interested in leisure, the harbor and the streets and a face in the crowd, and treats the festival as something that happened to a place, weather with a schedule. Eighty-two minutes. The National Film Registry keeps it, and part of the reason is plainly documentary: a particular week, a particular shoreline, an afternoon of American ease.

The usual arrangement runs the other way: here it is the girl who brings the boy into the racket. She grew up inside a mob and knows the terms; he comes out of a circus. Rouben Mamoulian made it in 1931, when the talking gangster picture was months old and its grammar was being settled one release at a time, and reviewers put it among the year's ten best. The eighty-three minutes belong less to gunfire than to a courtship warped by proximity to money. Bootlegging is the family business. So the question the film keeps returning to is domestic: whether two people can walk into it side by side and come out as the same two people, and what a father does with a daughter who has arranged the recruitment herself.

A schoolgirl is killed on Confederate Decoration Day, and a small-town lawyer with Senate ambitions grasps immediately that what he needs is not a culprit but the right culprit. The right one is a northerner who taught her at the business school where she died, and the evidence against him will remain circumstantial for the length of the case. Mervyn LeRoy's 1937 film is about manufacture: a prosecutor and a reporter working the same story from opposite ends until a town's stock of grievance has a face to fasten on. It is cold about how fast this can be arranged, and precise about who collects at each stage. The setting is southern, the machinery is not; it requires only a holiday, a dead girl, an outsider, and a newspaper with columns to fill by morning.

Porgy gets around by goat cart, and the neighborhood's opinion of him is settled before he sings a note. Catfish Row is an invented block of Charleston, a fishing community around 1900, and exact about hierarchy: who works the docks, who begs, who is feared. Otto Preminger runs it 138 minutes as sung drama, so bargaining, gossip and threats all arrive in full voice, which changes what a quarrel between neighbors sounds like. The love story is a triangle held together by dependence. Bess is bound to the stevedore Crown by fear and to Porgy by something milder, and neither bond is presented as a choice freely available to her. Hollywood staged this material in 1959 with all the assurance and all the difficulty that implies. The National Film Registry keeps it, difficulty included.

The honeymoon in Spain falls through, so the marriage starts in his parents' house, thin walls and all. British comedy in 1967 could still draw most of its material from a young couple unable to get a room to themselves, and Roy Boulting spends nearly two hours on what follows: gossip in a small town, a father with opinions and no sense of when to withhold them, weeks in which a private difficulty turns into public property. What keeps it out of farce is the amount of embarrassment it is prepared to sit inside. Arthur and Jenny still have to go to work in the morning among people who have theories about them, and the film understands that the wisecrack and the wound arrive together, from the same mouths, usually over breakfast.

Forty-five minutes, one aircraft, one target: the submarine pens at Wilhelmshaven. William Wyler's documentary was assembled in 1944, while the campaign it describes was still being flown, and it works less as the account of a raid than as an account of the hours before one. The briefing, the weather, the checks, a crew who know each other's habits and are about to spend a morning in thin metal over Germany. The B-17 was called a Flying Fortress, and the film lets the word fortress sit there unexamined while the guns are loaded. Some of it instructs and some of it is unmistakably first-hand. The brevity is part of the effect: no arc to speak of, only a job with a departure time and men who have to be somewhere at it.

David is well liked and not much relied upon, which in a mountain village amounts to a verdict on a boy. The mail has to get through; his brother cannot carry it, so David does, and the route runs past the Hatburns. Henry King builds the whole ninety-four minutes out of chores and proximity, a farm, a road, a sack of letters, a family nobody wants to cross, so that violence arrives as an interruption of work rather than as an adventure. Silent rural melodrama usually asks to be forgiven its simplicity. This one earns its plainness through specifics: what a smallholding requires by daylight, how quickly a reputation sets, why a mail sack weighs more than its contents to the person carrying it. It is David's standing among his neighbors, not the feud, that the 1921 film is actually about.

The marriage left two archives: his became literary history, hers became a medical file. Brian Gilbert puts Vivienne Haigh-Wood at the center of a story usually told from the other side, and much of the two hours concerns what her body did and how the men around her elected to interpret it, a gynaecological condition read as temperament, temperament read as madness. T. S. Eliot's fame grows in the meantime, and with it the number of people whose interests depend on the household staying quiet. Both leading performances drew Academy Award attention. The film keeps the furniture of English period drama, drawing rooms and doctors' appointments, but what it is really examining is authority: who is licensed to say what is wrong with someone, and what that license lets them do next.

The figures announce, in comic-strip balloons, that they are going to move, and then they do. Winsor McCay was drawing Little Nemo for the New York Herald when he made this, and the film keeps the newspaper's habits: the panel, the balloon, the joke told at the drawing's own expense. Twelve minutes, 1911, and no story worth the name. What there is instead is stretching, ballooning, folding, bodies behaving like rubber because nothing had yet ruled that they could not. The thing also went out under a longer name, Winsor McCay, the Famous Cartoonist of the N.Y. Herald and His Moving Comics, which is less modest than the drawings. The National Film Registry holds it. The pleasure is a man showing his hand on purpose, letting the trick be seen and then performing it anyway.
